### Observed differences

- Work on six activities — A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 — was reallocated between resources. In the earlier window, User_18 was the single largest performer on these activities, handling about 8–11 in 100 assignments, with the remainder spread over several other resources at roughly 3–12 in 100 each; in the later window, User_18's share fell to about 4–6 in 100 and the other formerly leading resources lost similar ground [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006].
- In the later window, User_35 (about 8–11 in 100) and User_15 (about 8–9 in 100) lead these activities after not appearing among the leading resources before (below about 3 in 100); the long-tail "other" share stayed roughly stable, at about 39–47 in 100 before and 43–47 in 100 after [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006].
- The shift has the same shape in all six activities (allocation dissimilarity 0.33–0.38, each larger than in more than 99.9% of random re-splits), with each profile resting on roughly 106–263 traces per window [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006].
- The elapsed time between consecutive completions on the A04→A01 pair shortened: the mean fell from about 48 hours to about 24 hours, the median from about 32 to about 25 hours, the 75th percentile from about 46 to about 35 hours, and the spread narrowed markedly (standard deviation about 71 to about 31 hours), based on 200 intervals in each window [TWAIT001].
- For context, screening found no qualifying control-flow differences (0 items against about 0.16 expected by chance), while the time family produced 1 item against about 0.017 expected and the resource family 6 items against about 0.005 expected [TWAIT001, ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006].

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that resource allocation changed: execution of A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was handed from one group of resources to another, with User_18 and the other formerly leading resources losing roughly half or more of their share while User_35, User_15 and other previously minor resources became the main performers [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]. Supporting signs: all six allocation profiles moved in the same direction with the same gaining and losing resources, suggesting one handover rather than six unrelated shifts; the resource family produced 6 qualifying items against about 0.005 expected without change; and no control-flow differences qualified, making a routing change unlikely. Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous, so no roles can be inferred, and the evidence cannot distinguish a deliberate reassignment of the same work from a changed mix of work reaching these activities.

Other differences: the A04→A01 completion-to-completion time roughly halved and became much less variable; the time family's single item also exceeds its chance expectation (1 against about 0.017), so a change in timing is a plausible second hypothesis in its own right, but nothing in this evidence links it to the reallocation [TWAIT001].
